quizzes.title: Court of Arbitration findings: MCQ
quizzes.passage:
The Court of Arbitration, which sits in The Hague, examined a dispute over the Indus Waters Treaty. The dispute followed India's decision to place the treaty in abeyance after the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack. The case raised a basic legal question: can one party step away from a treaty because of a security crisis, or must the treaty's own terms and the wider law of treaties decide the matter?

The ruling turned on the text of the treaty. The tribunal looked at the provisions on the Western Rivers, the rivers whose waters are central to the case. It also examined whether the treaty has any rules on terrorism or the use of force, since those issues sat in the background of the dispute.

The ruling also concerned a hydroelectric project on the Chenab. The tribunal placed interim limits on certain work at one of these projects, the Ratle project. Those limits are tied to a later stage of the dispute, which involves a technical expert appointed under the treaty.

India has not accepted the ruling. Its government says the tribunal was constituted improperly and has no authority over its sovereign decisions or its projects on the western rivers. The disagreement therefore covers both the substance of the treaty and the legitimacy of the forum that decided it.

questions.q: Which 1969 convention did the tribunal apply in holding that India's abeyance decision was not permissible?
options: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties
questions.explanation: The ruling applied the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969 when holding the abeyance impermissible.

questions.q: Article III(1) of the Indus Waters Treaty obliges India to let flow the waters of which rivers to Pakistan?
options: All the rivers of the Indus basin
questions.explanation: Article III(1) obliges India to let the waters of the Western Rivers flow to Pakistan.

questions.q: What do the tribunal's interim limits on the Ratle project bar?
options: All hydropower generation at the project
Concreting of specified parts of the dam wall and power intake beyond prescribed levels
Any release of water into the Chenab
Any survey work for future projects
questions.explanation: The interim limits bar concreting specified parts of the dam wall and power intake beyond prescribed levels.

questions.q:
Read the assertion and reason below.
Assertion (A): The tribunal held that India's decision to place the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance was not permissible.
Reason (R): The treaty gives India no unilateral mechanism to suspend its treaty obligations.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
questions.explanation: The finding that no unilateral suspension route exists is the reason given for holding the abeyance impermissible.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Article III(1)   ->   A. Obliges India to let flow Western Rivers waters to Pakistan
II. Ratle project   ->   B. Interim limits on concreting specified parts of the dam wall
III. Cross-border terrorism   ->   C. Not accepted as a material breach by the tribunal
IV. Abeyance of the treaty   ->   D. Held not permissible under the treaty or international law

Choose the correct matching.
questions.explanation: Each item is paired with the provision or finding that the ruling and booklet attach to it.

questions.q:
Read the following statements about the tribunal's ruling:
I. The tribunal held that the treaty gives India no unilateral mechanism to suspend its obligations.
II. The tribunal held that the treaty contains provisions on terrorism and the use of force, so cross-border terrorism was a material breach.
III. The tribunal held that India's abeyance decision was permissible under the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Only the first statement matches the ruling, since the treaty has no terrorism provisions and abeyance was held impermissible.

questions.q:
How many of the following statements about the ruling are correct?
The tribunal said the treaty continues to apply.
The tribunal found that the abeyance decision was permissible under international law.
The tribunal said the interim limits on the Ratle project last until a set period after the Neutral Expert's final determination.
The tribunal imposed interim limits on the Kishenganga project.
questions.explanation: The first and third statements match the ruling, while the second and fourth do not.

quizzes.title: Court of Arbitration findings: TITA
quizzes.passage:
A ruling from an international Court of Arbitration has placed the Indus Waters Treaty at the centre of a fresh dispute between India and Pakistan. The treaty has governed the sharing of the Indus river system since 1960, and the question now is whether India could suspend it after a security crisis in 2025. The case asks whether a treaty can be set aside on that basis, or whether it keeps applying until the parties end it through a formal agreement.

The tribunal read the treaty as written and tested India's position against the wider law of treaties. It also considered whether the treaty's text deals with the use of force. These points matter because the answer shapes how the treaty's obligations on the Western Rivers are understood. The ruling is therefore a test of how the treaty's text applies to a new situation.

The ruling also touched on the Ratle project, a hydroelectric scheme in Jammu and Kashmir. Interim limits were placed on some work there, and those limits remain linked to a later stage of the dispute.

India has rejected the ruling and does not accept the tribunal's authority over its decisions on the western rivers. Its objections focus on the tribunal's standing and on the path the dispute took before the tribunal was asked to decide it.

questions.q: Under which article of the Indus Waters Treaty is India obliged to let flow the waters of the Western Rivers to Pakistan? (give the article with its number)
questions.explanation: Article III(1) requires India to let the waters of the Western Rivers flow to Pakistan.

questions.q: Which 1969 convention did the tribunal apply to hold that the abeyance was not permissible? (short name)
questions.answer: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties
accept: Vienna Convention on Law of Treaties
Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969
questions.explanation: The tribunal applied the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969 in its ruling.

questions.q: In which city is the Court of Arbitration based? (city name)
questions.explanation: The Court of Arbitration is a Hague-based tribunal, as the booklet describes it.

questions.q: On which river is the Ratle hydroelectric project located? (river name)
questions.explanation: The Ratle hydroelectric project is located on the Chenab River in Jammu and Kashmir.

questions.q: Which body issued the ruling, known by its initials? (initials only)
questions.explanation: The booklet refers to the ruling as the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) ruling at The Hague.

questions.q: Does the treaty contain any provisions dealing with terrorism or the use of force? (answer yes or no)
questions.explanation: The tribunal observed that the treaty contains no provisions dealing with terrorism or the use of force.

questions.q: What term describes India's decision to temporarily suspend the treaty? (one word)
questions.explanation: The booklet uses the term abeyance, meaning temporary suspension or disuse, for India's decision.

quizzes.title: India's objection to the tribunal: MCQ
quizzes.passage:
The Indus Waters Treaty is an agreement between India and Pakistan on the river system of the Indus basin. Its rules cover how the waters are shared, and it also sets out how disagreements are to be handled. That second part has become the focus of a recent dispute, because India has rejected a ruling from an international tribunal and has questioned whether the tribunal should have been formed at all.

The debate turns on the structure of the treaty. The two countries read its disputes process differently, and the answer affects which forum can hear a particular question. Each reading leads to a different view of whether the tribunal had any role to play. Both sides refer to the same treaty text, and they differ in how they read it. This difference in reading is at the heart of the dispute.

Parallel moves also matter. In the years before the ruling, both sides pursued processes at the same time, and the institutions involved had to decide how those processes could coexist. That history has given the dispute a procedural side, separate from the questions about water.

India's objections therefore concern procedure, legitimacy and the reach of the tribunal, rather than the flow of the rivers themselves.

questions.q: India's Ministry of External Affairs says the Court of Arbitration was constituted by which body, contrary to the treaty?
questions.explanation: The Ministry of External Affairs says the World Bank constituted the Court of Arbitration contrary to the treaty.

questions.q: In India's view of the treaty's dispute route, which step comes immediately after the Permanent Indus Commission?
questions.explanation: India's graded sequence sends technical differences from the Commission to a Neutral Expert before any legal dispute.

questions.q: Which Indian ministry rejected the ruling?
questions.explanation: The Ministry of External Affairs rejected the ruling on behalf of the government.

questions.q:
Read the assertion and reason below.
Assertion (A): India has not taken part in the Court of Arbitration proceedings.
Reason (R): India maintains that the tribunal lacks jurisdiction over its sovereign decisions and infrastructure projects on the western rivers.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: India stayed out of the Court of Arbitration proceedings because it maintains that the tribunal lacks jurisdiction, so R explains A.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Pakistan's 2016 proceedings   ->   A. Sought establishment of a Court of Arbitration
II. India's 2016 request   ->   B. Appointment of a Neutral Expert to examine technical aspects
III. Ministry of External Affairs   ->   C. Said the tribunal was constituted contrary to the treaty
IV. Abeyance decision   ->   D. Remains valid after the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack, according to New Delhi

Choose the correct matching.
questions.explanation: Each item is matched to the action or statement that the booklet reports for it.

questions.q:
Read the following statements about India's position:
I. India has recognised the legitimacy of the tribunal but has not participated in its proceedings.
II. In 2016, India requested the appointment of a Neutral Expert to examine technical aspects of the dispute.
III. According to New Delhi, the abeyance decision after the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack remains valid.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements II and III are reported in the booklet, while India has not recognised the tribunal's legitimacy.

questions.q:
How many of the following statements are correct?
India has neither recognised the tribunal's legitimacy nor participated in its proceedings.
According to India's Ministry of External Affairs, the Court of Arbitration was constituted by the United Nations.
In 2016, Pakistan initiated proceedings seeking a Court of Arbitration.
questions.explanation: The first and third statements are correct, while the second wrongly names the United Nations.

quizzes.title: India's objection to the tribunal: TITA
quizzes.passage:
A recent ruling has pushed the Indus Waters Treaty back into the news, and with it the question of how disagreements under the treaty should be settled. The treaty contains its own dispute-resolution structure, and the current controversy is about whether that structure was followed. One side has rejected the outcome and has challenged the authority of the tribunal that issued it.

The dispute has a history. Parallel processes were opened in the same period, and the institutions that oversee the treaty had to decide how those processes could run side by side. At one point both were paused, and later both were allowed to move forward again.

The tribunal's findings and the response to them have renewed interest in the treaty's design. The question is not only about how water is allocated but also about process, including which step must come before another and which forum has the final word.

India's government has defended its decision on the treaty and says the tribunal has no power to review it. The dispute therefore turns as much on the order of steps as on the water itself. Several steps in the process are described as separate stages, each with its own role.

questions.q: After the Permanent Indus Commission, which body takes up technical differences under India's reading of the treaty? (name the body)
questions.explanation: Under India's reading, technical differences go from the Commission to a Neutral Expert before any legal dispute.

questions.q: Which Indian ministry said the Court of Arbitration was constituted contrary to the treaty? (give the abbreviation)
questions.explanation: The Ministry of External Affairs made this statement in rejecting the ruling.

questions.q: According to India's government, which institution constituted the Court of Arbitration? (name)
questions.explanation: India's Ministry of External Affairs says the World Bank constituted the tribunal contrary to the treaty.

questions.q: India's abeyance decision followed which April 2025 terror attack? (place name)
questions.explanation: New Delhi says its abeyance decision after the Pahalgam terror attack of April 2025 remains valid.

questions.q: India argues the tribunal lacks jurisdiction over its sovereign decisions and infrastructure projects on which group of rivers? (two words)
questions.explanation: India says the tribunal has no jurisdiction over its projects on the Western Rivers.

questions.q: In 2016, which country initiated proceedings seeking a Court of Arbitration? (country name)
questions.explanation: In 2016, Pakistan initiated proceedings seeking the establishment of a Court of Arbitration.

questions.q: Did India take part in the Court of Arbitration proceedings? (answer yes or no)
questions.explanation: India did not participate in the Court of Arbitration proceedings, although it took part in the Neutral Expert process.

quizzes.title: Indus river system: MCQ
quizzes.passage:
The Indus river system is one of the great river systems of South Asia, and its waters are shared by more than one country. The system is made up of a main river and several large tributaries, and each of these rises in a different part of the mountains. Some tributaries begin in high passes and glaciers, while others rise from springs in valleys below.

Because the rivers cross political borders, the way their waters are used is a matter of law as well as geography. Over time, countries and international bodies have developed rules on how shared waters should be managed. These rules cover the use of water in a shared basin and the wider conduct of states that share a watercourse.

The Indus Waters Treaty divides the rivers into two groups, and each group carries different rights for India. The eastern rivers are open to Indian use, while the western rivers are allocated primarily to Pakistan. India keeps some rights over the western rivers, subject to the treaty's conditions.

The booklet describes each river by its sources and by the points where it joins another river. The main tributaries named in the booklet are the Jhelum, the Chenab, the Ravi, the Beas and the Satluj, and each has its own course.

questions.q: Which international instrument codified law on the non-navigational uses of international watercourses in 1997?
options: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties
questions.explanation: The UN Watercourses Convention of 1997 codified law on non-navigational uses of international watercourses.

questions.q: The Indus is said to originate at which glacier near Mt Kailash?
questions.explanation: The Indus originates at the Bokhar Chu Glacier near Mt Kailash in Tibet.

questions.q: The Chenab joins which river at Panchnad?
questions.explanation: The Chenab joins the Satluj at Panchnad in Punjab, Pakistan.

questions.q:
Read the assertion and reason below.
Assertion (A): The Indus is a trans-boundary river.
Reason (R): The Indus empties into the Arabian Sea near Karachi.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but the outflow into the Arabian Sea does not explain why the Indus is trans-boundary.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Jhelum   ->   A. Rises at the Verinag Spring in the Kashmir Valley
II. Ravi   ->   B. Rises in the Kullu Hills near Rohtang Pass
III. Satluj   ->   C. Rises from the Manasarovar-Rakas Lakes in Tibet
IV. Chenab   ->   D. Originates near Bara Lacha Pass in Lahul-Spiti

Choose the correct matching.
questions.explanation: Each river is matched to its source as the booklet describes it.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about international rules on shared waters:
I. The Helsinki Rules of 1966 were adopted by the International Law Association.
II. The Helsinki Convention of 1992 provides a framework for preventing and controlling water pollution across national borders.
III. India, China and Pakistan have all signed the UN Watercourses Convention of 1997.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: India, China and Pakistan have not signed the UN Watercourses Convention, so the third statement is wrong.

questions.q:
How many of the following statements are correct?
The Indus is the longest river in Pakistan.
The Jhelum joins the Chenab at Trimmu.
The Satluj joins the Indus at Panchnad.
The Beas joins the Satluj at Harike.
questions.explanation: The Satluj joins the Indus above Mithankot, not at Panchnad, so three of the four statements are correct.

quizzes.title: Indus river system: TITA
quizzes.passage:
A trans-boundary river system needs rules that every country sharing it can accept. The Indus is one of the most significant examples in South Asia, and its basin is shared by several countries. Its main river rises far to the north, and several large tributaries join it from different directions across the region.

The tributaries have their sources in different places. Some begin in high mountain passes and frozen ice fields, while others come from springs or lakes in the mountains. As they flow, they meet one another at points along the plains, and some of these meeting points lie in Punjab.

Legal thinking about shared rivers developed over several decades. Early work set out principles for the use of water in a shared drainage basin. Later agreements dealt with other concerns, as well as with the wider law governing the non-navigational use of international watercourses.

Not every country has joined the most widely discussed of these agreements. The status of signatures shows which states have accepted the broader framework and which have stayed outside it. The main rivers of the system, including the Jhelum, the Chenab, the Ravi, the Beas and the Satluj, each have their own sources and meeting points.

questions.q: The Indus originates at which glacier near Mount Kailash in Tibet? (name of the glacier)
questions.explanation: The Indus originates at the Bokhar Chu Glacier near Mt Kailash, Mansarovar, in Tibet.

questions.q: The Jhelum joins the Chenab at which place in Punjab, Pakistan? (place name)
questions.explanation: The Jhelum joins the Chenab at Trimmu in Punjab, Pakistan.

questions.q: Near which pass do both the Ravi and the Beas have their source region? (name the pass)
questions.explanation: The Ravi rises in the Kullu Hills near Rohtang Pass, and the Beas originates near Rohtang Pass.

questions.q: The Satluj joins the Indus a little above which town in Punjab, Pakistan? (town name)
questions.explanation: The Satluj joins the Indus a little above Mithankot in Punjab, Pakistan.

questions.q: In which year was the UN Watercourses Convention adopted? (four-digit year)
questions.explanation: The UN Watercourses Convention was adopted in 1997 and codified law on non-navigational uses of international watercourses.

questions.q: Which body adopted the Helsinki Rules of 1966? (give the abbreviation)
questions.explanation: The Helsinki Rules of 1966 were adopted by the International Law Association.

questions.q: The Helsinki Convention of 1992 provides a framework for preventing and controlling what, across national borders? (one word)
questions.explanation: The Helsinki Convention of 1992 provides a legal framework for preventing and controlling water pollution across national borders.
